name: Zoe Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies or government. Your answers stay confidential; there is no right view here. What does an ordinary workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 27 and lead a small wedding quartet, though the title sounds richer than it is. I also teach violin and record short parts for local projects.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the day do you like, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A pupil finally hearing her own clean note is the best bit. My music master’s degree did not teach me how to chase a late invoice without sounding desperate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a normal Tuesday I teach scales in the church hall, rehearse a wedding quartet, then send invoices from my kitchen table. I love hearing a shy pupil find a clear note, but chasing late fees wears me out. I’d say AI Plateau changes little for our quartet. A cheap booking form might spare a few emails, but the chairs still need players.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the thin month is the problem, not the software. A cancelled wedding can leave rent short even when AI turns out to be mostly hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep teaching my six regular pupils and take the quartet bookings already on the calendar. Starting this week, I’d put ten from each lesson payment into a rent envelope if the pupil actually pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy, even with the same work. A late invoice can still make the landlord’s reminder feel very loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a cancelled wedding mean in cash?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One Saturday fee is about a third of my rent. I would ask the venue for its deposit before I order sheet music.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the booking software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our cellist would have to try the booking software first and show that it saves time. I have never used an AI tool, and my pupils should not be test cases.

say: Quartet work would still need **players** in the room, even if booking emails become easier.
I’d tell pupils the **lessons** still depend on listening, practice and a person who knows their hands.
think: My **rent** depends on weekend fees and pupils paying on time, with almost no money behind me.
A small software saving will not fix the **late invoices** that already interrupt my sleep.
do: Keep the **six pupils** on their usual lesson slots and honour the quartet dates already booked.
Put **ten** from each paid lesson into a rent envelope, if the payment actually arrives.
feel: I feel **uneasy** because one cancellation can still leave a hole in the rent.
fieldNote: Her public **confidence** in live playing covers a worry rooted in unpredictable fees, not a belief that AI has arrived.
The rent **envelope** is conditional on getting paid, and she refuses an untested tool rather than all future change.
S0.quote: A cancelled wedding can leave rent short even when AI turns out to be mostly hype.

steps.text: Keep teaching six regular pupils and honour booked quartet dates
Put ten from each paid lesson into a rent envelope

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The morning would still start with the church hall, but fewer parents might call about lessons. I’d watch whether the wedding coordinator replaces musicians with generated tracks. At rehearsal I’d say Steady Disruption should make booking quicker, and a live quartet is still worth paying for. I would tell the other players to ask for clear deposits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, music for adverts and cheap receptions may go first. Grocery money comes from little recording fees that a machine could erase before anyone cancels a concert. A shrinking list of pupils would hurt too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d ask the coordinator which bookings have real musician fees and require deposits for new dates. In the first year of a drop, I’d offer a Saturday beginner group at the hall, if four families sign up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about the recording work. My hands can play, but someone can press a button and sell a track before I finish packing the violin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many families would make the group work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four paying families would cover the hall hire and leave enough for my morning. Without four paid places, I would keep the usual lessons instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound certain about live music; why add a class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The live quartet is my craft, but recordings also pay for groceries. I cannot let pride decide whether the rent gets paid.

say: I’d tell the quartet to protect **deposits** as cheap tracks reach reception bookings.
I’d still explain why a **live performance** matters to families who choose one.
think: Small **recording fees** buy groceries, and AI music could remove them before live bookings change.
I fear fewer **pupil calls** if families spend less on music generally.
do: Ask the wedding **coordinator** which dates still carry musician fees and require deposits on new dates.
Offer a Saturday **beginner group** if four families agree to pay and cover the hall.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing grocery money from recordings while rent remains fixed.
fieldNote: She can defend live music while admitting the less visible **recording fees** are her immediate exposure.
Her group lesson idea has a **four-family** threshold; she does not claim demand she has not checked.
S1.quote: Grocery money comes from little recording fees that a machine could erase before anyone cancels a concert.

steps.text: Require deposits for new wedding quartet dates
Offer Saturday group if four paying families cover hall hire

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be at the hall in 2028 with a bow in my hand, but the emails about recordings might stop. Around 2031, if robots can play hands-on music as well, even that stage would be under pressure. I’d tell the quartet that AGI by 2028 is a hard blow to paid music, and we should hold our existing dates. I wouldn’t promise anyone the wedding work is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The recording jobs and perhaps the composition work from my master’s degree could go first. In 2028, an empty recording calendar could arrive three years before any robot picks up a violin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d call each venue this month about deposits and ask the hall whether families still want in-person lessons. If recording fees vanish in the first year after 2028, I’d cut my studio rental and teach at the hall only.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed, because two years is no time to build savings from what I earn. I picture opening an empty calendar and finding the rent is still due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which expense could you actually remove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio room costs a fixed sum every month. At the next renewal I could drop it and carry my violin to the hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to another city?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are few music jobs nearby, and I cannot afford another city’s deposit. If I lost the flat, I would ask my sister for a sofa while I looked for work.

say: I’d tell the quartet that **recording fees** could disappear by 2028, so confirmed dates matter.
I would not promise that **live bookings** remain safe when capable robots arrive around 2031.
think: My **master’s training** includes composition, which thinking AI could undercut before robots touch performance.
Two years of low fees cannot build the **cushion** I would need for a sudden loss.
do: Call each **venue** about deposits this month and ask the hall about in-person lesson demand.
Drop the rented **studio room** at renewal if recording work disappears after 2028.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by an empty 2028 recording calendar and the same rent bill.
fieldNote: She separates the **2028** loss of thinking work from the later threat to playing around 2031.
Dropping the studio is a **conditional** first-year cut; a move remains beyond her means unless the flat is lost.
S2.quote: In 2028, an empty recording calendar could arrive three years before any robot picks up a violin.

steps.text: Call wedding venues about deposits this month
Drop rented studio room at renewal if recording fees vanish

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With AGI by 2031 I would have five years to see the recording market change. The playing robot would follow around 2034, so teaching in person would still have a little more time. I’d tell pupils I’ll keep showing up, but that music work may look different by 2031. I’d ask parents to book a term at a time instead of promising years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could use those five years to build a steady teaching roster, though I dislike betting on a new platform. My degree and playing skill mean something to families, yet the low pay makes every experiment costly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next term I’d ask the hall whether one extra teaching afternoon is available if three pupils commit. In the first year after 2031, I’d keep the slot only while the pupils cover the room and turn down shorter recording jobs that pay less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, but not frozen. Five years lets me test the class without asking anyone to lend me money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why only one afternoon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need to keep the quartet weekends, so one extra afternoon is enough to test. Three paying pupils can buy me an afternoon of teaching; a promise about the future cannot pay for the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if families choose AI lessons too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some families may prefer AI lessons, and I cannot count them as future customers. I would keep teaching those who want someone in the room listening closely.

say: I’d tell parents my **in-person lessons** will continue while they are willing to book a term.
I’d explain that **recording work** may change by 2031 and hands-on playing faces robots around 2034.
think: Five years might let me grow **teaching income** before cheap generated music takes the recording fees.
I cannot afford a large **platform gamble** while my savings remain below one month of bills.
do: Ask the hall for one extra **teaching afternoon** next term if three pupils commit.
Keep that **hall afternoon** after 2031 only while three paid pupils cover the room.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though a five-year run-up gives me room to test one small change.
fieldNote: Her timetable shifts toward **teaching** while she guards quartet weekends and avoids paying for uncertain technology.
The extra afternoon depends on **three pupils**; she does not present a new roster as certain.
S3.quote: Three paying pupils can buy me an afternoon of teaching; a promise about the future cannot pay for the room.

steps.text: Add hall teaching afternoon if room available and three paid pupils cover it
Keep hall afternoon after 2031 if three paid pupils cover room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years sounds long from the hall doorway, though I would only be 37 in 2036. Thinking AI would take composition and recording first; robots capable of performance would come around 2039. I’d tell our quartet that AGI by 2036 gives us time to make the live work strong. I’d still ask every player to keep an honest record of fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could spend a decade teaching good habits and saving, if parents keep paying. I still fear a clever system could give away lessons and music, and my skill alone would not settle the rent. I would be 37 when thinking AI arrived in 2036, still young enough to teach but too old to live on promises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the six regular pupils, raise lesson fees only when the next term starts, and save half of any increase. In the first year after 2036, I’d review whether hall lessons still cover rent before taking a new studio lease.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy rather than frightened tonight. A decade gives me a chance to make a cushion, although my current bank balance is still thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a fee rise fair to families?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would give families a term of notice before raising the lesson fee. Anyone struggling could have their first lesson at the old rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hope to have by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six months of bills would feel enormous to me. I would start with one month and count only money that actually arrives.

say: I’d tell the quartet to strengthen **live bookings** and keep honest fee records during the longer run-up.
I’d explain that **thinking work** changes by 2036, with capable performance robots around 2039.
think: A decade could let me build **savings** from lessons if families keep paying.
My playing **skill** cannot pay rent alone if people stop buying music.
do: Keep the **six pupils** and give families a term of notice before any lesson fee rise.
Save **half** of any fee increase and review hall income before a studio lease after 2036.
feel: I feel **uneasy** because a long runway helps, while today’s bank balance remains thin.
fieldNote: She treats the decade as a chance to build a **cushion**, not proof that demand will survive.
A fee increase remains **conditional** and includes notice for families who may struggle.
S4.quote: I would be 37 when thinking AI arrived in 2036, still young enough to teach but too old to live on promises.

steps.text: Keep six pupils and give a term of notice before fee changes
Save half of any lesson fee increase

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because recording work could disappear before I can build even one month of rent. Deposits I can enforce and affordable hall space would help me keep teaching.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask how much a good player earns after the applause. The audience sees four people in neat black clothes, not four people splitting a fee and paying for travel.

headlineQuote: The audience sees four people in neat black clothes, not four people splitting a fee and paying for travel.
portrait: At **27**, Zoe leads a wedding quartet, teaches violin and records short parts after a music master’s degree.
Her **low pay** and less than one month of savings make cancelled fees a rent problem even in AI Plateau.
She resists untested **AI tools**, yet she will test a small teaching expansion if pupils cover the hall.
Fast **2028 AGI** threatens recordings first; capable robots around 2031 would threaten live playing later.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could empty her recording calendar before she saves one month of rent.
whatWouldHelp: Enforceable **deposits** and affordable hall space would let her keep earning through in-person lessons.
